precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.prompt: A client already pours coffee every morning and wants a vegetable habit. What does habit stacking look like in that routine?

options.a: Add vegetables, a walk, and a food log in the same first week
options.b: Pair each vegetable serving with dessert as an after-habit reward
options.c: Eat one vegetable right after the coffee they already make
options.d: Put every new habit in one app so tracking counts as stacking

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Habit stacking attaches one tiny new action to a cue that already happens. Coffee is the existing routine; the vegetable is the add-on. Stacking is not a pile of new behaviors, a dessert bargain, or an app. One linked action is easier to repeat than a week of simultaneous starts.

distractorExplanations.a: Loading several new habits in one week is overload, not stacking onto a single existing cue.
distractorExplanations.b: A dessert bargain is reinforcement after the fact; stacking uses an existing routine as the trigger.
distractorExplanations.d: A tracker is logging. Stacking is a behavior linked to a real-world cue, not an app grouping.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.prompt: A client’s usual habit is a 30-minute walk. After a brutal workday they say they cannot do it. What should they do today?

options.a: Skip the walk until a calmer day so they do not do it badly
options.b: Keep the full 30 minutes so the standard never drops
options.c: Walk twice as long tomorrow to repay today’s missed dose
options.d: Take a five-minute walk today so the pattern still happens

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: A bad-day version shrinks the habit so the streak survives. Five minutes still counts as showing up. Skipping until a “good” day, insisting on the full dose, or doubling tomorrow all turn one hard day into a break in the chain.

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting for a better day breaks the cue-routine loop; a tiny version keeps the identity of someone who walks.
distractorExplanations.b: Holding the full 30 minutes on a wrecked day invites a miss; shrink the dose instead of protecting an all-or-nothing standard.
distractorExplanations.c: Making it up later is compensatory thinking and often leads to another skip; do a smaller version now.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.prompt: A client grabs chips from a bowl on the counter every evening after work. Which change is environment design, not a pep talk?

options.a: Put protein or fruit in sight and store the chips away
options.b: Tape a willpower reminder to the fridge and leave the chips out
options.c: Send hourly phone alerts telling them to skip the chips today
options.d: Keep chips on the counter so they can practice saying no

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Environment design makes the wanted action the easy default and the unwanted one harder to start. Visible protein or fruit and hidden chips change the path of least resistance. Notes, hourly nags, and leaving the cue in place still rely on willpower against a loud snack cue.

distractorExplanations.b: A fridge note is a willpower prompt; the chips still sit in the visual field as the easy grab.
distractorExplanations.c: Phone alerts are monitoring, not a change to what is sitting on the counter when they walk in.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaving the chips out trains cue-driven grabbing; environment work reduces the cue, it does not amplify it.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.prompt: A client wants to “become someone who cooks.” Which identity line is actually backed by a tiny proof?

options.a: Post “lose 20 pounds by June” as a deadline on the fridge
options.b: Say “I cook on Sundays” and roast one pan as proof today
options.c: Repeat “I have to stop junk food” as a daily restriction
options.d: Repeat “I am a meal-prep person” with no cooking this week

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Identity-based change is a who-I-am statement plus a small action that proves it. Roasting one pan is evidence. Outcome deadlines, “have to stop” rules, and labels with no behavior do not build the identity of a cook.

distractorExplanations.a: A weight deadline is an outcome goal, not an identity plus a cooking rep.
distractorExplanations.c: A prohibition is restriction language; identity work is “I’m someone who cooks,” not “I must stop junk.”
distractorExplanations.d: A self-label without a cooking action is wishful branding; identity follows evidence.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.prompt: A client is ravenous at night, skipping training, and missing check-ins after several 5-hour nights. Why treat sleep as part of nutrition coaching?

options.a: Sleep is where most of the day’s calories get burned
options.b: Sleep work matters mainly for clients chasing muscle gain
options.c: Short nights raise hunger and break training and food habits
options.d: Coaches should diagnose apnea before changing any meals

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Sleep is a nutrition habit because it changes appetite, recovery, and whether food practices stick. Short nights commonly drive late hunger and missed sessions. Coaches ask about sleep and refer medical red flags; they do not treat sleep as a calorie furnace or diagnose apnea.

distractorExplanations.a: Resting metabolism is modest; sleep’s coaching value is hunger, training quality, and adherence, not extra calorie burn.
distractorExplanations.b: Appetite, recovery, and consistency matter for fat-loss and health clients too, not mainly hypertrophy.
distractorExplanations.d: Suspected apnea is a referral, not a coach diagnosis, and it is not a prerequisite for discussing sleep timing.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.prompt: After tense meetings a client finishes a bag of snacks at the desk and calls themselves weak. How should the coach frame it?

options.a: Push through the meetings with stricter willpower at the desk
options.b: Cut 300 daily calories so the snack bag still “fits”
options.c: Label it binge-eating disorder and pause all food coaching
options.d: Call it a missing pause skill and practice one replacement

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Stress-eating is usually a skills gap: no pause, no other downshift, easy food nearby. Teach a tiny replacement (stand up, protein, a short walk) rather than a character attack. Restriction and armchair diagnoses usually make the loop worse; refer if true eating-disorder signs persist.

distractorExplanations.a: Calling it weak willpower ignores the missing coping skill and leaves the cue-food loop in place.
distractorExplanations.b: A tighter calorie target adds stress and often worsens desk snacking instead of teaching a pause.
distractorExplanations.c: Occasional stress-eating is common; coaches do not diagnose disorders from one pattern and should refer if red flags continue.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.prompt: It is Sunday’s check-in. What should a weekly habit review actually ask?

options.a: What worked, what blocked them, and one next tweak
options.b: How many rules they broke and why they failed again
options.c: Which three new habits they should add starting Monday
options.d: What the scale did so the calorie target can be reset

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: A useful weekly review is a short retrospective: keep what worked, name the blocker, pick one next tweak. Shame audits, stacking three new habits, and letting the scale set calories all pull attention off the tiny behavior that needs to stick.

distractorExplanations.b: Counting broken rules is a compliance trial; it breeds shame instead of locating one workable next action.
distractorExplanations.c: Adding several habits at once overloads capacity; the review chooses one change, not a new stack.
distractorExplanations.d: Scale-led retargeting is outcome tinkering; the review first looks at behaviors and barriers.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.prompt: A client has a wedding dinner Saturday and asks how to “stay on plan.” What is the habit-friendly move?

options.a: Skip social meals until they reach the goal weight
options.b: Eat protein first, pick one treat, stop when satisfied
options.c: Eat almost nothing all day to bank calories for dinner
options.d: Fast the next morning to cancel Saturday’s extra food

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Life is the program: plan the meal instead of deleting it. Protein first, one chosen treat, and stopping when satisfied is a skill they can reuse. Avoidance, all-day restriction, and next-day fasting teach a restrict-then-overdo cycle.

distractorExplanations.a: Banning social meals until a number on the scale is not a lasting habit; the skill is showing up with a simple plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Banking calories usually backfires as overeating at the event; eat normally and use a protein-first plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Compensatory fasting after the fact turns one dinner into a restrict-binge loop; resume the next meal as usual.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.prompt: A client wants daily weigh-ins to “stay honest.” How should the coach treat the number?

options.a: Weigh once a month so the number cannot cause stress
options.b: Judge the whole week by the lowest morning weigh-in
options.c: Treat the scale as one data point next to habits
options.d: Weigh after the biggest meal to see the “true” number

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Weight is noisy (food, water, hormones). It is useful as one data point beside adherence, measurements, photos, and how they feel—not as a daily verdict. Frequency is secondary to how the number is interpreted; post-feast weigh-ins just capture a full gut.

distractorExplanations.a: Monthly weighing can hide trends; the issue is treating the scale as a verdict, not that daily data is forbidden.
distractorExplanations.b: Making the lowest weigh-in the week’s grade is the trap; context from habits and other measures matters more.
distractorExplanations.d: Weighing after a large meal mainly shows food and water, not fat change, and trains panic about a fake high.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.prompt: A client ate extra dessert at lunch and wants to scrap the rest of the day. What is the slip skill?

options.a: Throw out the plan and restart from next Monday
options.b: Skip dinner tonight to offset the extra dessert
options.c: Wait until tomorrow morning to start the day clean
options.d: Eat the next planned meal as they normally would

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Slips are expected. The skill is resuming at the next meal, not a Monday reboot, a skipped dinner, or a “clean” tomorrow. One extra dessert becomes a lost day only if the client extends it on purpose.

distractorExplanations.a: A single slip is not a reason to scrap the plan; restarting Monday turns one lunch into a wasted week.
distractorExplanations.b: Skipping dinner to compensate starts a restrict-then-overdo cycle; eat the next meal as planned.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting for tomorrow converts one dessert into a full off-plan evening; the next meal is the reset.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.prompt: A client muted the habit app after hourly pings. What should the coach do with reminders?

options.a: Use fewer cues anchored to real moments in their day
options.b: Keep hourly pings because repetition builds discipline
options.c: Add more alerts so they cannot forget the habit
options.d: Randomize ping times so the surprise keeps them honest

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Cues work when they are few and tied to a real routine (after coffee, after parking). Hourly or random nags create mute-and-ignore. Discipline is not built by notification volume; it is built by a reliable context cue.

distractorExplanations.b: Hourly repetition usually produces alert fatigue and muting, not a durable habit.
distractorExplanations.c: More alerts after a mute is the same failed strategy with extra noise.
distractorExplanations.d: Random timing is harder to attach to a routine; a stable cue in the day is easier to keep.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.prompt: A client will take a 10-minute walk after dinner but refuses gym cardio. Why keep the after-meal walk?

options.a: It burns enough calories to replace their lifting sessions
options.b: It often eases glucose spikes and is easy to repeat daily
options.c: They should skip it because walking after eating hurts digestion
options.d: Keep the walk only if they already have diagnosed diabetes

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: A short post-meal walk is a tiny, repeatable activity habit. It commonly blunts glucose rises and is easy to stack after dinner. It is not a substitute for resistance training, not harmful digestion advice, and not only for people with diabetes.

distractorExplanations.a: Light walking does not replace the strength stimulus of lifting; keep both jobs separate.
distractorExplanations.c: Gentle walking after a meal is well tolerated for most people; it is not a digestion hazard to avoid.
distractorExplanations.d: Glucose and consistency benefits show up for many clients, not only those with a diabetes diagnosis.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.prompt: A client has a 40-page gourmet grocery PDF and still orders takeout. What should you coach instead of another meal-plan dump?

options.a: Hand them a longer gourmet PDF with foods they never cook
options.b: Shop with no list so they intuit better choices in the aisle
options.c: Make a short list from three meals they will cook this week
options.d: Ban grocery trips and put them on a full meal-delivery plan

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Grocery skill is buying what this week’s tiny cooking habit needs. A short list from three meals they will actually cook beats a unused PDF, aisle improvisation, or outsourcing the whole kitchen. Environment starts at the store, not in a 12-week menu they will never follow.

distractorExplanations.a: A longer unused PDF is the same failure mode: a plan they will not cook still leaves an empty fridge.
distractorExplanations.b: No list usually recreates last week’s takeout and impulse snacks; the skill is a list tied to real meals.
distractorExplanations.d: Delivery can be a short patch, but defaulting to a ban skips the grocery skill the habit depends on.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.prompt: A client is consistent Monday–Friday, then “blows it” all weekend. Which structure treats Saturday as part of the habit, not a blackout?

options.a: Keep weekdays strict and treat the whole weekend as off-plan
options.b: Cut weekday calories in advance to pre-pay for restaurants
options.c: Repeat the same four meals and ban every meal out
options.d: Keep a default breakfast and plan one meal out

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Weekends need a simple structure: a default breakfast or lunch they always do, plus one planned meal out. That keeps consistency without a 48-hour off-plan. All-off weekends, pre-cutting calories, and banning restaurants all fail as lasting habits.

distractorExplanations.a: A fully off-plan weekend often undoes five days of practice; plan the predictable chaos instead.
distractorExplanations.b: Banking weekday calories sets up overeating when they sit down; defaults plus one planned meal work better.
distractorExplanations.c: Banning meals out is brittle; the skill is one planned restaurant meal inside an otherwise normal day.

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.prompt: A client rates “vegetables at every lunch” a 2 out of 10 for confidence. What do you do to the habit?

options.a: Add a second habit so they feel momentum despite the 2/10
options.b: Shrink the action until they rate it about 8/10 confident
options.c: Use the 2/10 score as a shame cue so they take it seriously
options.d: Raise their calorie-burn target because the food habit is too hard

precision-nutrition-l1-readiness-check-h.explanation: Size the habit to confidence. A 2/10 means the action is too big; shrink it (one vegetable at one meal) until they feel about 8/10 likely to do it. Adding more habits, shaming the score, or swapping to extra cardio all ignore the sizing problem.

distractorExplanations.a: A second habit on top of a 2/10 action increases load; shrink first, do not stack more.
distractorExplanations.c: Shame does not raise confidence; it usually makes the client hide misses instead of shrinking the task.
distractorExplanations.d: Raising a burn goal does not fix an oversized food habit; the move is a smaller vegetable action.
